title: Understanding Quality Control Orders: Mandatory vs Voluntary Standards
text: Indian Standards formulated by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) are fundamentally voluntary in nature to encourage continuous quality improvement and technological standardization. However, under Section 16 of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016, the Central Government (through line ministries such as DPIIT, Ministry of Steel, MeitY, MoRTH, and Ministry of Consumer Affairs) has the statutory power to issue Quality Control Orders (QCOs) in the Official Gazette. A QCO makes compliance with specific Indian Standards legally compulsory for the protection of human, animal, or plant health, environmental safety, national security, or prevention of deceptive practices. Once a QCO takes effect, no enterprise may manufacture, import, store, sell, or distribute non-certified goods. Non-compliance is a punishable offense under the BIS Act, carrying severe financial penalties, seizure of consignments, and imprisonment up to two years.

title: Scheme-I (ISI Mark) vs Scheme-II (CRS): Key Operational Differences
text: BIS operates multiple conformity assessment pathways tailored to industry characteristics. Scheme-I (Product Certification Scheme) is the traditional ISI Mark scheme. It requires the manufacturer to maintain complete in-house testing equipment, execute a formal Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT), and undergo a mandatory physical factory audit by BIS officers who inspect manufacturing lines and draw verification samples. Once granted, products bear the iconic ISI monogram with a Certification Marks Licence (CML) number. In contrast, Scheme-II (Compulsory Registration Scheme - CRS) was established in collaboration with MeitY for fast-moving electronics and IT hardware. Scheme-II does not require a pre-grant factory inspection; instead, manufacturers submit type-test reports from BIS-recognized NABL laboratories along with a formal self-declaration of conformity. Products certified under CRS carry the standard BIS CRS border logo with an assigned R-number.

title: Step-by-Step BIS Manakonline Application Process for Domestic Manufacturers
text: Domestic manufacturers applying for a BIS licence under Scheme-I utilize the centralized Manakonline portal (manakonline.in). The procedure comprises eight structured stages: (1) Profile registration and digital signature verification on the portal. (2) Selection of the relevant Indian Standard and product sub-type. (3) Preparation of technical documentation including factory machinery layout, list of in-house testing equipment with calibration certificates, manufacturing process flow charts, and raw material test certificates. (4) Formulation of the in-house Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT). (5) Submission of Form V online alongside statutory application fees. (6) Deputation of a BIS Technical Officer for a physical factory inspection, verifying production capability and testing sealed factory samples. (7) Independent testing of sealed samples at a BIS or BIS-recognized laboratory. (8) Scrutiny of audit reports and grant of the CML licence upon payment of marking fees.

title: Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme (FMCS) Requirements and Process
text: Foreign manufacturers exporting goods covered under mandatory QCOs to India must obtain a BIS licence under the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme (FMCS). The foreign entity must establish an Authorized Indian Representative (AIR) who is a resident citizen of India, legally responsible for ensuring compliance and handling regulatory correspondence. The application process requires submission of comprehensive manufacturing plant details, factory quality manuals, and payment of statutory audit and inspection fees. BIS technical officers travel to the foreign manufacturing facility to conduct an on-site audit, inspect quality controls, and seal production samples for testing in designated BIS laboratories in India. Licences under FMCS are granted initially for one to two years and require a performance bank guarantee.

title: The BIS Laboratory Recognition Scheme (LRS) and NABL Interoperability
text: Under the BIS Laboratory Recognition Scheme (LRS), 2020, BIS grants recognition to external commercial, academic, and government testing laboratories to evaluate samples drawn during licence processing and post-market surveillance. A prerequisite for BIS recognition is valid accreditation by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) in accordance with ISO/IEC 17025 for the specific Indian Standards involved. Laboratories are audited by BIS assessment teams to verify equipment accuracy, environmental conditioning chambers, proficiency testing participation, and competence of testing personnel. Test reports issued by recognized laboratories via the digital BIS Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) are legally binding evidence for conformity assessments.

title: Understanding the Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT) for Factory QA
text: Every licence under Scheme-I operates under a product-specific document known as the Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT). The SIT defines the minimum level of quality control that a manufacturer must maintain continuously on the shop floor. It categorizes testing into three distinct tiers: (1) Raw Material Tests: Verification of incoming inputs against approved supplier certificates or incoming inspection logs. (2) Routine Tests: 100% inspections performed on every manufactured unit to ensure immediate consumer safety (e.g. electrical flash insulation test on mixers, hydrostatic pressure test on pressure cookers). (3) Acceptance Tests: Lot-wise sampling tests carried out on batches before dispatch to verify statistical conformity (e.g. tensile pull of steel rebars, optical transmittance of visors). The manufacturer must record all test results in indelible registers and retain records for at least three years.

title: Consumer Guide to Gold Hallmarking and 6-Digit HUID Verification
text: Gold Hallmarking in India is governed under the Bureau of Indian Standards (Hallmarking) Regulations, 2018. Since June 2021, mandatory hallmarking has been enforced in over 343 notified districts across India. Genuine hallmarked gold jewellery bears three mandatory laser-engraved symbols: (1) The official triangular BIS Logo. (2) Purity in Karat and Fineness (e.g., 24K995 for 99.5% pure, 22K916 for 91.6% pure, 18K750 for 75.0% pure, 14K585 for 58.5% pure). (3) The 6-digit alphanumeric Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) code. The HUID is unique to each piece of jewellery and is assigned by BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs). Consumers can verify the legitimacy of any gold ornament instantaneously using the 'Verify HUID' feature in the BIS Care mobile app, which reveals the registered jeweller name, AHC registration, date of hallmarking, and exact tested fineness.

title: Using 'Know Your Standard' (KYS) to Identify Applicable Indian Standards
text: The BIS 'Know Your Standard' (KYS) portal is an open digital repository designed to help industry professionals, MSMEs, and researchers locate relevant standards. Users can search by standard number, product keyword, technical committee, or Harmonized System (ITC-HS) tariff classification code. For each standard, the KYS directory provides the active status, year of publication, technical division, scope narrative, price group, active amendments, and whether the standard is covered under an active or upcoming Quality Control Order. KYS also provides links to draft standards open for public comments during the consensus development stage, allowing manufacturers to participate in standards formulation.

title: MSME Concessions, Fee Discounts, and Extended QCO Compliance Timelines
text: Recognizing the vital role of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in the Indian economy, the Ministry of Consumer Affairs and line ministries offer substantial concessions for BIS compliance. Under the revised fee schedule, Micro enterprises receive up to an 80% concession on application and annual minimum marking fees, while Small enterprises receive a 50% concession, provided they possess a valid Udyam Registration Certificate. Furthermore, modern Quality Control Orders issued by DPIIT and Ministry of Steel feature staggered enforcement timelines: large manufacturers must comply upon the initial date, while Small enterprises receive an additional 6 months, and Micro enterprises receive an additional 12 months buffer to establish in-house test infrastructure without business disruption.

title: BIS Care App: How Consumers Can Verify ISI Marks, CML Licences, and Report Violations
text: The BIS Care mobile application, available on Android and iOS in bilingual Hindi and English, empowers consumers to verify the authenticity of certified products before purchasing. Through the 'Verify Licence (CML)' module, users input the 7-to-10 digit licence number displayed beneath the ISI mark to confirm the registered manufacturer's name, brand name, validity status, and certified product scope. The 'Verify R-Number' module provides similar verification for electronic goods certified under Scheme-II (CRS), while 'Verify HUID' verifies hallmarked gold jewellery. The application also provides an encrypted grievance registration system enabling consumers to lodge official complaints regarding substandard goods, unauthorized misuse of the ISI mark, or misleading claims, triggering inspection by BIS enforcement officers.

title: Guidelines for Standard Mark (ISI Monogram) Embossing and CML Labeling
text: The Bureau of Indian Standards (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018 govern the visual representation and placement of the Standard Mark. The iconic ISI monogram must maintain exact geometric proportions as prescribed in the First Schedule. The Certification Marks Licence number (CML XXXXXXX) and the applicable Indian Standard number (e.g. IS 2347) must be indelibly printed, engraved, or embossed adjacent to the mark. For durable goods such as pressure cookers, steel bars, and vehicle helmets, the mark must be stamped or molded onto the product body so that it remains visible throughout the product's design life. False application or imitation of the Standard Mark is a criminal offense subject to statutory enforcement action.

title: BIS Market Surveillance, Sample Seizure, and Penal Provisions under BIS Act 2016
text: To protect consumer welfare and uphold fair competition, the Enforcement Directorate of BIS conducts systematic market surveillance across factory premises, wholesale hubs, and retail outlets. BIS enforcement officers possess search and seizure powers under Section 28 of the BIS Act, 2016. When counterfeit ISI marks or non-compliant mandatory QCO goods are discovered, enforcement squads execute search and seizure raids, impounding stock and initiating prosecution in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate. Under Section 29, manufacturing or selling goods in contravention of a mandatory QCO is punishable by imprisonment up to two years or a fine of up to ten times the value of the non-compliant goods or both.

title: What is BIS? The Bureau of Indian Standards — Mandate, History and Functions
text: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is India's national standards body, established as a statutory body under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 (replacing the earlier BIS Act, 1986). BIS operates under the administrative control of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. Its primary mandate is to formulate and promote Indian Standards, operate product certification and conformity assessment schemes, provide hallmarking services for precious metals, run laboratory testing facilities, and protect consumer interests. BIS has its headquarters in Manak Bhavan, New Delhi, and maintains five regional offices (Northern, Eastern, Western, Southern, and Central) and branch offices across major industrial and commercial centres. BIS also represents India in international standardisation bodies such as ISO (International Organization for Standardization) and IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission). Standards formulated by BIS are published as Indian Standards (IS) and are numbered sequentially. BIS is funded through government grants, licence fees from certified manufacturers, and revenue from selling standards documents.

title: Overview of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016
text: The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 is the primary legislation governing BIS operations. It replaced the BIS Act, 1986 and significantly expanded BIS powers. Key provisions include: Section 14 — grants BIS authority to operate product certification and conformity assessment schemes; Section 16 — empowers the Central Government to issue Quality Control Orders (QCOs) making compliance with Indian Standards mandatory for specified products; Section 17 — governs hallmarking of articles made of precious metals; Section 28 — grants enforcement powers including search, seizure, and inspection; Section 29 — prescribes penalties for contravening mandatory orders. The 2016 Act introduced compulsory hallmarking (not present in the 1986 Act), expanded the scope to include services and systems standards, and enabled electronic certification. The Conformity Assessment Regulations, 2018 and Hallmarking Regulations, 2018 were notified under this Act.

title: What is the ISI Mark? Meaning, History, and How to Recognise a Genuine Certificate
text: The ISI Mark (Indian Standards Institution mark) is India's most widely recognised product quality certification mark, awarded by BIS under Scheme I (Product Certification). The name traces back to the Indian Standards Institution, BIS's predecessor body. The ISI mark consists of a stylised hexagonal monogram. Products bearing this mark have been independently verified to conform to the relevant Indian Standard. The mark is accompanied by a Certification Marks Licence (CML) number unique to the manufacturer and product type, and the IS number of the applicable standard. Consumers should verify the CML number using the BIS Care app. Common products that must carry the ISI mark include pressure cookers, electrical appliances, steel bars, helmets, packaged drinking water bottles, and LPG cylinders. Approximately 33,000 ISI mark licences are active in India at any given time across over 900 product categories.

title: Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS): Electronic Products and IT Hardware
text: The Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS), known as Scheme II, was launched in 2012 in collaboration with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to regulate the safety and quality of electronic and IT hardware products sold in India. Unlike Scheme I (ISI Mark), CRS does not require a pre-grant physical factory inspection. Instead, manufacturers — both domestic and foreign — must submit type-test reports from BIS-recognised NABL-accredited test laboratories and execute a self-declaration of conformity. Upon approval, an R-number is assigned to the product model and manufacturer. The product must display the BIS CRS registration mark (a circle with 'R' and the registration number). Products covered include self-ballasted LED lamps, LED luminaires, laptops, tablets, mobile phone adapters, set-top boxes, power banks, and over 60 other electronic product categories. Foreign manufacturers must either set up a test facility in India or use a BIS-recognised lab. CRS registrations are valid for two years and must be renewed before expiry.

title: Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs): Role, Recognition, and HUID Process
text: Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (AHCs) are BIS-recognised facilities authorised to assay the purity of gold and silver articles and engrave the Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) code on each piece. AHCs are assessed and recognised by BIS under the Hallmarking Regulations, 2018. To be recognised, an AHC must have a fire assay or XRF spectrometry facility meeting ISO/IEC 17025 calibration standards. Every AHC is assigned a unique four-digit AHC code by BIS. The hallmarking process involves: (a) Jeweller submits articles to AHC. (b) AHC assays purity using fire assay or XRF. (c) AHC engraves the BIS Hallmark consisting of the BIS logo, purity in karat/fineness, and a six-character alphanumeric HUID. (d) Hallmarking record is uploaded to the BIS HUID portal in real time. As of 2024, there are over 1,400 BIS-recognised AHCs across India. Hallmarked jewellery can be verified by consumers using the 'Verify HUID' feature in the BIS Care app.

title: How Indian Standards Are Developed: Technical Committees and Public Participation
text: Indian Standards are developed through a consensus-based process managed by BIS Technical Committees (TCs) and Subcommittees. Committees are organised by technical domains into Division Councils, such as the Electrotechnical Division Council (ETDC), Chemical Division Council (CDC), Civil Engineering Division Council (CEDC), and Mechanical Engineering Division Council (MEDC). Each committee includes representation from industry, consumer organisations, academic institutions, research bodies, and government departments. The standards development cycle includes: (a) Identification of need and project approval. (b) Formation or assignment to a technical committee. (c) Preparation of draft standard by working groups. (d) Wide circulation for public comment (Draft for Comments, DC phase) — open to any stakeholder. (e) Balloting and consensus resolution. (f) Final publication as an IS. The typical cycle takes 18–36 months. Stakeholders can participate in public comments through the BIS website during the DC phase. Standards are periodically reviewed every five years (quinquennial review) and may be reaffirmed, revised, or withdrawn.

title: Renewal, Suspension, and Cancellation of BIS Certification Marks Licences
text: A BIS Certification Marks Licence (CML) under Scheme I is granted with an annual renewal requirement. Renewal involves: (a) Payment of the Annual Minimum Marking Fee (AMMF), calculated based on the quantum of production marked during the year. (b) Submission of updated in-house test records and calibration certificates for testing equipment. (c) Satisfactory outcome of the latest BIS surveillance inspection report. BIS conducts surprise surveillance visits (typically one to four times per year depending on risk category) to verify ongoing compliance with the Scheme of Inspection and Testing (SIT). If violations are found — such as non-maintenance of test records, use of out-of-calibration equipment, or substandard samples — BIS may issue a Notice of Suspension. Continued violations result in CML Cancellation. Cancelled licences are published on the BIS portal and affected manufacturers must cease using the ISI mark immediately. Reinstatement after suspension requires compliance verification by BIS officers and payment of reinstatement fees.

title: Import Restrictions for Products Under Mandatory Quality Control Orders
text: When a Quality Control Order (QCO) is issued for a product category, the restrictions apply equally to domestic manufacturing and imports. Imported products covered by a mandatory QCO must carry a valid BIS certification mark (ISI mark for Scheme I products, or CRS R-number for Scheme II electronics) before they can be customs-cleared. Foreign manufacturers must obtain BIS certification under either the Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS) or the Foreign Manufacturers Certification Scheme (FMCS) depending on the applicable scheme. Customs officers at ports of entry verify BIS certification status through the BIS LIMS and Manakonline portals. Non-compliant imports may be detained, recalled, or destroyed at the importer's expense. The DPIIT QCO portal maintains a consolidated list of all active QCOs including their coverage of imports. Certain categories may qualify for conditional test import provisions (for type-testing purposes only) under DPIIT notifications.

title: BIS Regional and Branch Offices Across India
text: BIS maintains five Regional Offices to extend certification, testing, and consumer protection services across India: (1) Northern Regional Office (NROL) — Chandigarh, covering Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Delhi, and Rajasthan. (2) Eastern Regional Office (EROL) — Kolkata, covering West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, Assam, and North-East states. (3) Western Regional Office (WROL) — Mumbai, covering Maharashtra, Gujarat, Goa, and Madhya Pradesh. (4) Southern Regional Office (SROL) — Chennai, covering Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. (5) Central Regional Office (CROL) — Delhi, handling central administration, appeals, and national-level coordination. In addition, BIS operates over 35 Branch Offices in industrial cities for processing licence applications, conducting factory inspections, and handling consumer complaints. The BIS Central Laboratory is co-located with the Northern Regional Office in Ghaziabad.

title: Scheme X: BIS Management System Certification (ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 22000)
text: BIS offers Management System Certification under Scheme X, providing third-party certification to organisations wishing to demonstrate compliance with internationally recognised management system standards. BIS is one of India's leading certification bodies for ISO 9001 (Quality Management System), ISO 14001 (Environmental Management System), ISO 22000 (Food Safety Management System), ISO 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety), and ISO/IEC 27001 (Information Security Management). BIS management system audits are conducted by accredited lead auditors and assessed by the National Accreditation Board for Certification Bodies (NABCB). Certificates are valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits. BIS Scheme X certification is widely recognised in government procurement and is a prerequisite for participation in several GeM (Government e-Marketplace) tenders. Applications are submitted through the BIS portal and processed by the BIS headquarters Management System Certification section.
